steps.premise: A visitor may want to identify a pen by the line it produced.
steps.action: Tag each pen with its model and nib size.
steps.consequence: The visitor can remember which pen they liked.
steps.quote: Label each pen with its model and nib size. A visitor who likes a particular line can then remember exactly which pen made it.

steps.premise: Paper texture affects how a nib feels.
steps.action: Give all visitors the same paper for their initial trials.
steps.consequence: They can compare nibs without mistaking coarse paper for a scratchy nib.
steps.quote: Give everyone a strip cut from the same paper for the first comparison. A rougher sheet at one seat won't get mistaken for a scratchier nib.

steps.premise: A visitor wants a pen for a particular planner.
steps.action: Let them test the pen on a page of their own planner too.
steps.consequence: They can judge its performance on the paper they use.
steps.quote: Someone choosing a pen for a daily planner needs to know how it behaves on those pages. Leave room for them to try a few words in their own planner as well.

steps.premise: A visitor puts a pen down to look at the marks it made.
steps.action: Set the pens in shallow trays with grooves.
steps.consequence: The pen stays in place instead of rolling off.
steps.quote: Arrange the pens in shallow grooved trays. A visitor can set one down to inspect the writing without having it roll onto the floor.

steps.premise: Caps on different models open in different ways.
steps.action: Indicate next to each pen how its cap comes off.
steps.consequence: Even a new user can open it gently.
steps.quote: Some caps pull straight off while others unscrew. Mark the opening motion beside each pen so a first-time user can get it open gently.

steps.premise: A fountain pen writes with just its own weight.
steps.action: Show that on scrap paper before passing the pen to a beginner.
steps.consequence: The beginner can write with a light touch.
steps.quote: A fountain pen can make a line under its own weight. Demonstrate that on a scrap before handing it over so a newcomer can start without bearing down on the nib.

steps.premise: The visitor is comparing several pens.
steps.action: Have them write the same familiar wording with each pen.
steps.consequence: They can feel how their usual handwriting compares without composing a new line for every pen.
steps.quote: Let each person write a familiar phrase with several pens. They'll know how their usual lettering feels without having to think up a fresh sentence each time.

steps.premise: A writer may brush their hand over fresh ink.
steps.action: Time the sample and swipe it at successive intervals.
steps.consequence: The writer can see how long the ink needs to dry.
steps.quote: Set a timer beside a wet ink sample and make a fresh swipe at intervals. A visitor who tends to drag a hand across the page can see how long the ink takes to set.

steps.premise: An uncovered nib can dry out between turns.
steps.action: Have each visitor put the cap back on when they finish.
steps.consequence: The next writer receives a pen with a usable nib.
steps.quote: A cap left off while people talk can leave the next visitor with a dry nib. Give the person finishing a turn the job of recapping the pen.

steps.premise: Caps can get mixed up when people put them down together.
steps.action: Use matching removable markings on a cap and its barrel.
steps.consequence: Volunteers can return each cap to its pen.
steps.quote: Match a removable mark on each cap to one on its barrel. If two caps get laid down together, volunteers can reunite them with the right pens.

steps.premise: A pen is running low and its owner knows how to fill it.
steps.action: Ask the owner to top it up at a separate table.
steps.consequence: Others can keep using the writing seats.
steps.quote: Have the owner refill a pen at a side table when its ink runs low. The owner knows its filling mechanism, and the writing seats stay open for the other pens.

steps.premise: Ink can drip as visitors pass pens around.
steps.action: Cover the trial surface with a mat that washes clean.
steps.consequence: Someone can wipe away a drop before it marks the furniture.
steps.quote: Put a washable mat under the tryout area. A drop that escapes while someone passes a pen can be wiped up before it stains the furniture.

steps.premise: A few loops may hide discomfort from writing for longer.
steps.action: Make room for visitors to write a paragraph.
steps.consequence: They can assess how the grip feels over time.
steps.quote: A couple of ordinary loops can feel comfortable even with a pen that's tiring over time. Offer enough space to write a full paragraph and judge the grip.

steps.premise: A left-handed writer prefers the outside position at a shared table.
steps.action: Offer them the leftmost seat.
steps.consequence: They have room to move their elbow as they write.
steps.quote: Seat a left-handed writer at the left end of a shared table when they prefer it. Their elbow then has room to move through a line.

steps.premise: Several visitors want to try the same pen.
steps.action: Provide a sign-up sheet for that pen.
steps.consequence: People can try others while keeping their turn in the queue.
steps.quote: Use a sign-up slip for a particularly popular pen. Visitors can try something else and still keep their place for a turn.

steps.premise: A visitor likes an ink color but may want another pen body.
steps.action: Name each pen's ink on its sample card.
steps.consequence: The visitor can identify the bottle to look for.
steps.quote: List the ink in each pen on the sample card. Someone admiring the color can find the right bottle even if they prefer a different pen body.

steps.premise: The borrower wants to feel the weight of a cap on the back of a pen.
steps.action: Indicate which owners allow visitors to post the cap.
steps.consequence: Visitors can test the added weight on an approved pen.
steps.quote: Show which pens the owners are happy to have used with the cap on the back. Visitors can explore how the extra weight feels without guessing what a borrowed pen will tolerate.

steps.premise: Fine edges can look solid from a distance.
steps.action: Place a magnifier near the writing samples.
steps.consequence: Visitors can see details at the edges of thin lines.
steps.quote: Offer a hand lens beside the finished samples. A visitor can inspect the edges of a fine line that looks solid at arm's length.

steps.premise: A pen skips or loses ink.
steps.action: Provide a labeled tray for the faulty pen.
steps.consequence: Another visitor can choose a working pen while a volunteer checks the fault.
steps.quote: Set out a clearly marked tray for a pen that skips or leaks. The next person can pick a working pen while a volunteer looks into the trouble.

steps.premise: The session is ending and lenders are reclaiming pens.
steps.action: Have lenders sign their initials as they collect their pens.
steps.consequence: Organizers can find unclaimed pens while the lenders are still present.
steps.quote: Ask lenders to initial their pens back out at closing. The organizer can spot a pen still waiting in its tray while its owner is nearby.
